title: Jev for lead scoring
summary: Rank inbound leads by fit and intent before a human looks at them.
fits_when: You get more inbound leads than your team can read, and most are low value.
Your ideal customer profile fits in a few plain sentences.
You want a ranked queue for reps, not a fully automated decision on who gets contacted.
avoid_when: You need a written rationale for each score. Jev returns scores and probabilities, not explanations.
The score depends on data Jev can't see, such as CRM deal history, and you can't include it in the input.

title: Jev for email triage
summary: Sort mail into categories, rate urgency and flag what needs a reply.
fits_when: You or your team spend real time deciding what to open first.
Your categories are stable (for example: needs reply, updates, promotions, sales, spam).
A human stays in the loop for anything consequential.
avoid_when: You want replies drafted. Jev can't generate text; pair it with a language model for the emails that need one.
Your privacy obligations don't allow sending email content to a third-party API.

title: Jev for support ticket routing
summary: Send each ticket to the right queue and flag frustrated customers.
fits_when: You have three or more queues and tickets regularly land in the wrong one.
Keyword-based routing rules keep breaking.
You want early warning on angry or at-risk customers.
avoid_when: You have a single support queue, so there's nothing to route.
You need a reply sent to the customer. That's a text-generation job.

title: Jev for content moderation
summary: Flag spam, abuse and prompt injection before content goes live.
fits_when: You need a cheap filter in front of user-generated content or an LLM agent.
Each policy can be expressed as a yes/no statement.
Probabilities feeding a human review queue work for you.
avoid_when: You need legally defensible moderation decisions with written reasoning.
The content is mostly images or video. Jev is built for text; image input is experimental.

title: Jev for research and news filtering
summary: Surface only the papers and headlines that match what you care about.
fits_when: You follow a feed (arXiv, RSS, news) that is mostly noise for you.
You can describe your interests in a paragraph.
Titles and abstracts are enough to judge relevance.
avoid_when: You need summaries of what you keep. That's a language model's job.
Relevance depends on reading full papers; cost rises with input length.

title: Jev for SEO search-intent classification
summary: Label keyword lists by intent and relevance, at any volume.
fits_when: You work with keyword exports of thousands of rows.
You want to cluster keywords by intent before writing anything.
avoid_when: You need search volume or difficulty. That data comes from SEO tools, not a model.

title: Jev for ad and creative classification
summary: Tag ads by angle and hook strength, and pre-check them against policy.
fits_when: You're analysing a large library of your own or competitors' ads.
You want consistent tags so you can compare angles against performance.
avoid_when: The creative is image- or video-only with little text.
You want new ad copy generated.

title: Jev for semantic search
summary: Re-rank search results by how well each one matches the query.
fits_when: Queries are written in natural language, not keywords.
A conventional search already produces a shortlist of candidates.
Each result has a short text description Jev can read.
avoid_when: You need to search millions of items directly. Jev evaluates one item at a time, so narrow the list first.
Results are mostly images.

title: Jev for agent and browser decisions
summary: Pick the next action in an agent loop in milliseconds.
fits_when: Your agent repeatedly chooses from a known set of actions or elements.
Latency matters: games, browsers, real-time systems.
You already use a language model for planning and want to cut its calls.
avoid_when: The step requires writing, coding or multi-step reasoning. Jev can't plan.
The set of possible actions isn't known in advance.

title: Jev for LLM guardrails
summary: Check every message and reply for jailbreaks and hazards before the LLM acts on it.
fits_when: You run an LLM app or agent and want your own rules, written where you can read them, not only the model maker's.
You want a check on every turn without paying for a second LLM call each time.
Different products need different strictness from the same assessment.
avoid_when: You need the reason a message was blocked written out for the user. Jev returns probabilities, not explanations.
A single check is your only safety layer for something dangerous. Keep hard rules in code too.

title: Jev for checking citations
summary: Catch made-up quotes and claims the source does not support.
fits_when: An LLM writes answers or reports with citations to documents you hold.
A wrong citation is costly: legal, medical, financial or technical writing.
You want people to check only the doubtful citations, not all of them.
avoid_when: You do not have the source documents. Jev can only judge a quote against the text you send it.
Quotes are loosely paraphrased. An exact string match marks those as made up, so you would need fuzzy matching first.

title: Jev for filtering RAG passages
summary: Drop irrelevant and poisoned passages before they reach the answering model.
fits_when: Your retrieval returns passages that read alike, so similarity scores cannot tell them apart.
Retrieved text can come from users or the web, where it may carry instructions aimed at the model.
Questions sometimes rest on a false assumption that the documents correct.
avoid_when: Your corpus is small, clean and written by you. A plain similarity search may be enough.
You need the passages rewritten or summarised. Jev only labels them; the language model writes.

title: Jev for re-ranking search results
summary: Score a shortlist against the query and put the best result first.
fits_when: Your search finds roughly the right documents but often not the best one first.
Relevance depends on meaning, not shared words: legal, support or product search.
You can keep the shortlist small (tens of results, not thousands).
avoid_when: Your keyword search already puts the right result first most of the time.
You need to score millions of documents per query. Re-rank a shortlist, not the whole index.

title: Jev for matching duplicate records
summary: Decide which records to merge, which to keep apart and which a person should check.
fits_when: Two sources describe the same things in different words: catalogues, CRMs, supplier lists.
A wrong merge is expensive, so you want a middle option that goes to a person.
A cheap first pass has already picked the pairs worth checking.
avoid_when: Records share a reliable ID. Match on the ID in code.
You need every pair in two large lists compared. Narrow the candidates first, then let Jev judge.

title: Jev for classifying documents into many categories
summary: Pick one of dozens of categories, and fall back to a broader one when unsure.
fits_when: Your categories form a hierarchy, so an unsure answer can fall back to the broader group.
There are many categories (Jev's Choice takes up to 255 options).
A broad but right label is more useful than a precise but wrong one.
avoid_when: Every document must get a precise label with no review. Plan for the unsure half.
Your labels are not described anywhere. Each option needs words that describe what belongs in it.

title: Jev for extracting dates, emails and amounts
summary: Find the right value in messy text without letting a model make one up.
fits_when: Documents contain several values of the same kind and the right one depends on the words around it.
A wrong digit is costly, so the value must be copied exactly from the text.
Dates appear in mixed forms, including relative ones such as 'tomorrow'.
avoid_when: The document has a fixed layout. A parser is cheaper and exact.
You need free-form text extracted (a summary, a reason). Jev picks from options; it does not write.
